Subtlety
sŭt´l-ty
n. (craft; artifice; fineness of contrivance used to deceive — the AV spells it subtilty)
Latin subtilis, finely woven, from sub tela, under the loom's warp — a thread so fine it is not seen. The serpent's quality in Genesis 3:1 is the first thing said about him.

Biblical Definition

Subtlety is craft too fine to be noticed. It is the serpent's first attribute: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made” (Gen 3:1). Paul fears its repetition: “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). He names it in a man to his face: “O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil” (Act 13:10). The armour is given against it: “that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph 6:11). And forewarning is the defence: “we are not ignorant of his devices” (2Co 2:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines subtlety as craftiness; cunning; artifice; and refinement; extreme acuteness, as the subtlety of an argument.

expand to see more

SUBTLETY, n. Thinness; fineness; exility; as the subtlety of air.

2. Refinement; extreme acuteness; as the subtlety of an argument or distinction.

3. Cunning; artifice; craftiness; guile.

SUBTILE, a. Thin; not dense or gross; sly in design; artful; cunning; insinuating.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:1 — "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?"

2Co 11:3 — "But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ."

Act 13:10 — "And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?"

Eph 6:11 — "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."

2Co 2:11 — "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices."

Modern Corruption

Temptation is expected to contradict Scripture, and the serpent's method was to quote it slightly wrong.

expand to see more

Genesis 3 repays close reading because nothing in it is a frontal attack. The serpent opens with a question and a misquotation just wide of the mark — Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? — which is not what God said, and which invites Eve to correct him and so to take up the position of adjudicating the command. Her reply adds a prohibition God never gave (neither shall ye touch it), and the ground has already shifted before any denial is offered. Only then comes ye shall not surely die, and by that point it lands on prepared soil.

Second Corinthians 11:3 tells us what the target is, and it is not doctrine in the first instance: your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. The word is singleness — an undivided attachment. Subtlety works by complication: adding a consideration, introducing a nuance, making a plain duty look naive, until a believer who could once have told you in a sentence what he owed his Lord now has a paragraph of qualifications. The corruption is of simplicity, and that is why it is so hard to see as loss; it feels like sophistication.

The defence Scripture gives is not cleverness. Second Corinthians 2:11 says we are not ignorant of his devices — the methods are documented, they are old, and they are in the Book. Ephesians 6 gives armour that is almost entirely defensive and entirely borrowed: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and one offensive weapon which is the word of God. That is exactly the weapon the Lord used in His own wilderness, against a tempter who by then had learnt to quote Scripture himself, and the difference was that He knew what the rest of the verse said.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arum (H6175), subtil, crafty, prudent; Greek panourgia (G3834), craftiness; methodeia (G3180), wiles, methods; noema (G3540), device, thought.

expand to see more

Hebrew arum (H6175) — subtil, crafty; Genesis 3:1 — the same word is rendered prudent in Proverbs 12:16, 14:15.

Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness; 2 Corinthians 11:3, 4:2, Ephesians 4:14, Luke 20:23.

Greek methodeia (G3180) — wiles, scheming methods; Ephesians 6:11, 4:14 — both occurrences.

Usage

"“Yea, hath God said…?” — a question, and a misquotation just wide of the mark."

"“Corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” — simplicity is the target."

"“We are not ignorant of his devices” — they are documented, and old."
